subject: math
title: Grade 8 Scientific Notation: Very Large and Very Small Numbers
seo_title: Grade 8 Scientific Notation Worksheets: Powers of Ten and Metric Prefixes, Free Math with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Represent and compare very large and very small numbers, including through the use of scientific notation, and describe various ways they are used in everyday life
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on scientific notation for the Ontario curriculum: powers of ten with positive and negative exponents, writing large and small numbers as a × 10ⁿ, comparing and ordering, and metric prefixes from pico to tera with space, cell and computer examples. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ, where a is at least 1 and less than 10: 3 200 000 = 3.2 × 10⁶ and 0.0045 = 4.5 × 10⁻³.
key_sub: The exponent is the number of places the decimal point moves, not the number of digits. Large numbers get a positive exponent and small numbers a negative one. 32 × 10⁵ is not scientific notation.
body_html:
Powers of ten

A positive exponent tells how many 10s you multiply: 104 = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000. A negative exponent means you divide by that many 10s. It gives a small positive number, not a negative number: 10−3 = 1 ÷ 1000 = 0.001.

PowerStandard formPowerStandard form
103100010−10.1
10210010−20.01
1011010−30.001
100110−60.000001

What scientific notation is

A number in scientific notation is written as a × 10n. The first factor a is at least 1 and less than 10. The exponent n is an integer. It is a short way to write very large and very small numbers, such as distances in space or the size of a cell.

Large numbers

Move the decimal point to the left until one non-zero digit is in front of it. The number of places you moved is the exponent.

Large number

The distance from Earth to the Sun is about 150 000 000 km. Write it in scientific notation.

Move the decimal point 8 places left: 1.5. The number is large, so the exponent is positive.

Answer: 1.5 × 108 km

Small numbers

For a number less than 1, move the decimal point to the right until one non-zero digit is in front of it. The exponent is negative.

Back to standard form

Write 7.1 × 10−4 in standard form.

Move the decimal point 4 places left, writing zeros: 7.1 → 0.00071.

Answer: 0.00071

Compare and order

Compare the exponents first: the greater exponent gives the greater number. Only when the exponents are equal do you compare the first factors.

Compare

Which is greater: 3.1 × 105 or 9.8 × 104?

The exponents are 5 and 4, and 5 > 4. Check: 310 000 > 98 000.

Answer: 3.1 × 105

With negative exponents, the exponent closer to zero gives the greater number: 2 × 10−3 = 0.002 is greater than 9 × 10−5 = 0.00009.

Metric prefixes

Each metric prefix stands for a power of ten. One step on this scale is 1000 times as large.

PrefixSymbolPower of tenExample
teraT1012a 2 TB hard drive
gigaG109128 GB of phone storage
megaM106a 3 MW wind turbine
microμ10−6a 2 μm bacterium
nanon10−9a 100 nm virus
picop10−121 ps = 10−12 s

faq.q: When do Ontario students learn scientific notation?
faq.a: In Grade 8. The Ontario math curriculum (Number, B1.1) has students represent and compare very large and very small numbers, including with scientific notation, and describe how they are used in everyday life.

faq.q: How do you write a small number like 0.0045 in scientific notation?
faq.a: Move the decimal point right until one non-zero digit is in front of it: 4.5. You moved 3 places, and the number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 4.5 × 10⁻³.

faq.q: Why is 32 × 10⁵ not in scientific notation?
faq.a: The first factor must be at least 1 and less than 10. 32 is too big, so write 32 as 3.2 × 10 and add 1 to the exponent: 3.2 × 10⁶.

faq.q: What do the prefixes mega, giga, micro and nano mean?
faq.a: Mega means 10⁶ (a million), giga 10⁹ (a billion), micro 10⁻⁶ (a millionth) and nano 10⁻⁹ (a billionth). Tera is 10¹² and pico is 10⁻¹².

sets.title: Powers of ten: positive and negative exponents

items.e: 10<sup>4</sup> = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10. That is 1 followed by 4 zeros (not 10 × 4).
10<sup>6</sup> = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10. That is 1 followed by 6 zeros (not 10 × 6).

items.q: Write 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 as a power of ten.
items.e: There are seven 10s multiplied together, so the exponent is 7: 10<sup>7</sup>.

items.q: Write 10 000 as a power of ten.
items.e: 10 000 is 1 followed by 4 zeros, so it is 10<sup>4</sup>. Count the zeros, not all the digits.

items.q: Write 100 000 000 as a power of ten.
items.e: 100 000 000 is 1 followed by 8 zeros, so it is 10<sup>8</sup>. Count the zeros, not all the digits.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1. Pattern: 10<sup>2</sup> = 100, 10<sup>1</sup> = 10, 10<sup>0</sup> = 1.
A negative exponent means divide: 10<sup>−2</sup> = 1 ÷ 100 = 0.01. It is a small positive number, not a negative number.
A negative exponent means divide: 10<sup>−5</sup> = 1 ÷ 100 000 = 0.00001. It is a small positive number, not a negative number.

items.q: Which number is the same as 10<sup>−1</sup>?
items.e: 10<sup>−1</sup> = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1. The minus sign in the exponent does not make the number negative.

items.q: Each tick on this scale is 10 times the tick to its left. Which number is at the red dot?
items.e: The dot is 2 ticks left of 10<sup>0</sup> = 1, so it is at 10<sup>−2</sup> = 0.01.

items.q: Each tick on this scale is 10 times the tick to its left. Which number is at the red dot?
items.e: The dot is 2 ticks right of 10<sup>0</sup> = 1, so it is at 10<sup>2</sup> = 100.

items.q: Write 0.001 as a power of ten.
items.e: Move the decimal point 3 places right to reach 1. So 0.001 = 10<sup>−3</sup>. Small numbers have negative exponents.

items.q: Write 0.000001 as a power of ten.
items.e: Move the decimal point 6 places right to reach 1. So 0.000001 = 10<sup>−6</sup>. Small numbers have negative exponents.

items.q: Write 11000 as a power of ten.
Which number is the same as 10<sup>−4</sup>?
items.e: 10−4 = 1 ÷ 104 = 110 000 = 0.0001.
10<sup>−1</sup> = 0.1 is the greatest. With negative exponents, the exponent closer to 0 gives the bigger number: 0.1 > 0.0001 > 0.0000001.
Multiplying by 10<sup>3</sup> moves the decimal point 3 places right: 4700.
Multiplying by 10<sup>5</sup> moves the decimal point 5 places right: 800 000.
Multiplying by 10<sup>−2</sup> moves the decimal point 2 places left: 0.062.
Multiplying by 10<sup>−4</sup> moves the decimal point 4 places left: 0.00039.
Move the decimal point 3 places left to get 2.4, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 2400 = 2.4 × 10<sup>3</sup>.
Move the decimal point 4 places left to get 4.5, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 45 000 = 4.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>.
Move the decimal point 5 places right: 2.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 250 000.
Move the decimal point 9 places right: 4 × 10<sup>9</sup> = 4 000 000 000.
Move the decimal point 6 places left to get 3.2, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 3 200 000 = 3.2 × 10<sup>6</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> fits. 32 × 10<sup>5</sup> is not: 32 is 10 or more.
Move the decimal point 4 places right: 1.36 × 10<sup>4</sup> = 13 600.
Move the decimal point 5 places left to get 5.07, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 507 000 = 5.07 × 10<sup>5</sup>.
Move the decimal point 6 places right: 7.08 × 10<sup>6</sup> = 7 080 000.
Move the decimal point 7 places left to get 1.2, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 12 000 000 = 1.2 × 10<sup>7</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 1.08 × 10<sup>8</sup> fits. 10.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> is not: 10.5 is 10 or more.
Move the decimal point 7 places right: 9.9 × 10<sup>7</sup> = 99 000 000.
Move the decimal point 6 places left to get 6.05, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 6 050 000 = 6.05 × 10<sup>6</sup>.
Move the decimal point 8 places left to get 8.7, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 870 000 000 = 8.7 × 10<sup>8</sup>.
Move the decimal point 11 places right: 6.4 × 10<sup>11</sup> = 640 000 000 000.

items.q: 32 × 10<sup>5</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 32 is 10 or more. 32 = 3.2 × 10<sup>1</sup>, so add 1 to the exponent: 5 + 1 = 6. Answer: 3.2 × 10<sup>6</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 9.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> fits. 72 × 10<sup>4</sup> is not: 72 is 10 or more.
Move the decimal point 10 places left to get 9.1, a number at least 1 and less than 10. So 91 000 000 000 = 9.1 × 10<sup>10</sup>.

items.q: 0.45 × 10<sup>7</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 0.45 is less than 1. 0.45 = 4.5 × 10<sup>−1</sup>, so subtract 1 from the exponent: 7 − 1 = 6. Answer: 4.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>.

items.q: 850 × 10<sup>3</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 850 is 10 or more. 850 = 8.5 × 10<sup>2</sup>, so add 2 to the exponent: 3 + 2 = 5. Answer: 8.5 × 10<sup>5</sup>.
Move the decimal point 2 places right to get 6. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.06 = 6 × 10<sup>−2</sup>.
Move the decimal point 2 places left, writing zeros as you go: 3 × 10<sup>−2</sup> = 0.03.
Move the decimal point 1 place right to get 3.05. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.305 = 3.05 × 10<sup>−1</sup>.
Move the decimal point 1 place left, writing zeros as you go: 6.08 × 10<sup>−1</sup> = 0.608.
Move the decimal point 3 places right to get 4.5. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.0045 = 4.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 4.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> fits. 45 × 10<sup>−3</sup> is not: 45 is 10 or more.
Move the decimal point 4 places left, writing zeros as you go: 7.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> = 0.00071.
Move the decimal point 2 places right to get 1.01. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.0101 = 1.01 × 10<sup>−2</sup>.
Move the decimal point 3 places left, writing zeros as you go: 5.25 × 10<sup>−3</sup> = 0.00525.
Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 7.2. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10<sup>−4</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 2.06 × 10<sup>−7</sup> fits. 0.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> is not: 0.5 is less than 1.
Move the decimal point 5 places left, writing zeros as you go: 1.4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> = 0.000014.
Move the decimal point 5 places right to get 8.9. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.000089 = 8.9 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.
Move the decimal point 6 places left, writing zeros as you go: 9.6 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 0.0000096.
Move the decimal point 6 places right to get 1.3. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.0000013 = 1.3 × 10<sup>−6</sup>.

items.q: Which number is written in scientific notation?
items.e: In scientific notation the first factor is at least 1 and less than 10. Only 7 × 10<sup>−2</sup> fits. 70 × 10<sup>−4</sup> is not: 70 is 10 or more.

items.q: 0.6 × 10<sup>−3</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 0.6 is less than 1. 0.6 = 6 × 10<sup>−1</sup>, so subtract 1 from the exponent: −3 − 1 = −4. Answer: 6 × 10<sup>−4</sup>.
Move the decimal point 7 places right to get 2. A small number has a negative exponent: 0.0000002 = 2 × 10<sup>−7</sup>.

items.q: 45 × 10<sup>−5</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 45 is 10 or more. 45 = 4.5 × 10<sup>1</sup>, so add 1 to the exponent: −5 + 1 = −4. Answer: 4.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>.

items.q: 0.25 × 10<sup>−6</sup> is not in scientific notation. Which number is equal to it and written in scientific notation?
items.e: 0.25 is less than 1. 0.25 = 2.5 × 10<sup>−1</sup>, so subtract 1 from the exponent: −6 − 1 = −7. Answer: 2.5 × 10<sup>−7</sup>.

sets.title: Compare and order numbers in scientific notation

items.e: Compare the exponents first. The greatest exponent is 5, in 3.1 × 10<sup>5</sup>. Only if two exponents are equal do you compare the first factors.
Compare the exponents first. The greatest exponent is 7, in 1.2 × 10<sup>7</sup>. Only if two exponents are equal do you compare the first factors.
3.7 × 10<sup>4</sup> = 37 000, which is between 10 000 and 100 000.
Compare the exponents first. The greatest exponent is −3, in 2 × 10<sup>−3</sup>. Only if two exponents are equal do you compare the first factors.
Compare the exponents: 5 > 4, so 4.2 × 10<sup>5</sup> > 9.7 × 10<sup>4</sup>. Check: 420 000 > 97 000.
4 × 10<sup>−3</sup> = 0.004, which is between 0.001 and 0.01.
Compare the exponents first. The greatest exponent is −2, in 6.4 × 10<sup>−2</sup>. Only if two exponents are equal do you compare the first factors.
Compare the exponents: −6 < −5, so 5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> < 5 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Check: 0.000005 < 0.00005.

items.q: 6 × 10<sup>7</sup> is how many times as large as 6 × 10<sup>4</sup>?
items.e: Divide the powers of ten: 10<sup>7</sup> ÷ 10<sup>4</sup> = 10<sup>3</sup> = 1000.
Compare the exponents first. The least exponent is −6, so 1.5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 0.0000015 is the least.
Write each number in standard form and compare: 9000 < 25 000 < 110 000. So the order is 9 × 10<sup>3</sup>, 2.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>, 1.1 × 10<sup>5</sup>.

items.q: 8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> is how many times as large as 8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>?
items.e: Divide the powers of ten: 10<sup>−3</sup> ÷ 10<sup>−5</sup> = 10<sup>2</sup> = 100.
Compare the exponents first. The least exponent is −3, so 7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> = 0.007 is the least.
Compare the exponents: −3 > −4, so 8.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> > 9.9 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Check: 0.0088 > 0.00099.
Write each number in standard form and compare: 0.00007 < 0.004 < 0.012. So the order is 7 × 10<sup>−5</sup>, 4 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, 1.2 × 10<sup>−2</sup>.

items.q: Which number is between 1 million (10<sup>6</sup>) and 1 billion (10<sup>9</sup>)?
9 × 10<sup>5</sup> is how many times as large as 3 × 10<sup>3</sup>?
items.e: Divide the first factors and the powers of ten: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 10<sup>5</sup> ÷ 10<sup>3</sup> = 100. 3 × 100 = 300.
The exponents are equal, so compare the first factors: 2.05 < 2.5.
Write each number in standard form and compare: 0.0000036 < 800 000 < 3 600 000. So the order is 3.6 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, 8 × 10<sup>5</sup>, 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup>.
Write each number in standard form and compare: 0.00055 < 0.0009 < 0.001. So the order is 5.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, 0.0009, 1 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.

items.q: The metric prefix mega (symbol M) means multiply by which power of ten?
items.e: Mega means 10<sup>6</sup> = 1 000 000.

items.q: The metric prefix micro (symbol μ) means multiply by which power of ten?
items.e: Micro means 10<sup>−6</sup> = 0.000001.

items.q: The metric prefix giga (symbol G) means multiply by which power of ten?
items.e: Giga means 10<sup>9</sup> = 1 000 000 000.

items.q: The metric prefix nano (symbol n) means multiply by which power of ten?
items.e: Nano means 10<sup>−9</sup> = 0.000000001.

items.q: The metric prefix tera (symbol T) means multiply by which power of ten?
The CN Tower in Toronto is 553 m tall. What is its height in scientific notation?
items.e: Move the decimal point 2 places left: 553 = 5.53 × 10<sup>2</sup> m.

items.q: The distance from Earth to the Sun is about 150 000 000 km. Which is this distance in scientific notation?
items.e: Move the decimal point 8 places left: 150 000 000 = 1.5 × 10<sup>8</sup> km. (1.5 × 10<sup>9</sup> comes from counting all 9 digits.)

items.q: The Moon is about 384 000 km from Earth. Which is this distance in scientific notation?
items.e: Move the decimal point 5 places left: 384 000 = 3.84 × 10<sup>5</sup> km.

items.q: Light travels about 3 × 10<sup>5</sup> km in one second. Write this distance in standard form.
items.e: 3 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 3 × 100 000 = 300 000 km. (15 comes from 3 × 5, which is not what 10<sup>5</sup> means.)

items.q: Canada has about 41 million people. Write this number in scientific notation.
items.e: 41 million = 41 000 000. Move the decimal point 7 places left: 4.1 × 10<sup>7</sup>.

items.q: A bacterium is about 2 micrometres (2 μm) long. How long is it in metres?
items.e: Micro means 10<sup>−6</sup>, so 2 μm = 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m. (10<sup>−3</sup> is milli and 10<sup>−9</sup> is nano.)

items.q: A red blood cell is about 8 μm wide. Write this width in metres as a decimal.
items.e: 8 μm = 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m. Move the decimal point 6 places left: 0.000008 m (5 zeros after the point).

items.q: Liam’s new hard drive holds 2 terabytes (2 TB). How many bytes is that?
items.e: Tera means 10<sup>12</sup>, so 2 TB = 2 × 10<sup>12</sup> bytes. (10<sup>9</sup> is giga and 10<sup>6</sup> is mega.)

items.q: A wind turbine in Ontario is rated at 3 megawatts (3 MW). How many watts is that?
A flu virus is about 100 nanometres (100 nm) across. Which is this length in metres, in scientific notation?
items.e: 100 nm = 100 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m = 10<sup>2</sup> × 10<sup>−9</sup> m = 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m. Add the exponents: 2 + (−9) = −7.

items.q: Maya’s phone has 128 gigabytes (128 GB) of storage. Which is this number of bytes in scientific notation?
items.e: 128 GB = 128 × 10<sup>9</sup> bytes. 128 = 1.28 × 10<sup>2</sup>, so the total is 1.28 × 10<sup>2 + 9</sup> = 1.28 × 10<sup>11</sup> bytes.

items.q: A human hair is about 80 μm wide. A bacterium is about 2 μm long. How many bacteria, end to end, would fit across the width of the hair?
items.e: Both lengths are in micrometres, so divide: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 bacteria.

items.q: A bacterium is about 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m long. A virus is about 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m across. The bacterium is how many times as long as the virus?
items.e: 2 ÷ 1 = 2 and 10<sup>−6</sup> ÷ 10<sup>−7</sup> = 10<sup>1</sup> = 10. 2 × 10 = 20 times as long.

items.q: A nanosecond is 10<sup>−9</sup> s and a picosecond is 10<sup>−12</sup> s. How many picoseconds are in one nanosecond?
items.e: 10<sup>−9</sup> ÷ 10<sup>−12</sup> = 10<sup>−9 − (−12)</sup> = 10<sup>3</sup> = 1000 picoseconds.

items.q: Canada has about 4 × 10<sup>7</sup> people and the world has about 8 × 10<sup>9</sup> people. The world population is about how many times as large as Canada’s?
items.e: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 10<sup>9</sup> ÷ 10<sup>7</sup> = 10<sup>2</sup> = 100. 2 × 100 = 200 times as large.
